meta.title: Dutch B2 Upper Intermediate
meta.subtitle: 1500 words · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Dutch → English (see the Dutch, recall the meaning) and English → Dutch (see an English meaning, recall the Dutch). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 1500 words of Dutch for an upper-intermediate learner, aligned to B2 of the Common European Framework of Reference, whose global descriptor begins 'Can understand the main ideas of complex text on both concrete and abstract topics, including technical discussions in his/her field of specialisation' — a learner here is able to interact with a degree of fluency and spontaneity that makes regular interaction with native speakers quite possible without strain for either party, and to produce clear, detailed text on a wide range of subjects and explain a viewpoint on a topical issue, giving the advantages and disadvantages of various options. The words already taught by the levels below this one are left out. WHERE THESE WORDS COME FROM, since it matters: Dutch has examinations at these levels — the inburgeringsexamen, the Staatsexamen NT2 and the CNaVT — but no graded word list for them was found published, so this deck is not any examination's vocabulary and does not claim to be. It is assembled from two things that can be stated. 354 of the 1500 come from a vocabulary written for the level's scope — work, business and the economy, politics, law and society, science and technology, the environment and climate, health and medicine, higher education, the media and the arts, abstract ideas and argument, the connectives of formal writing, character and behaviour, feelings and states of mind, the city and planning, and the verbs of getting things done — and the other 1146 are the commonest remaining words of everyday Dutch, taken from a frequency list built from film and television subtitles and counted by the WHOLE word, every form of a verb or an adjective added together. The cards are dealt by that frequency, so the words you meet most often come first. Every headword has its pronunciation beneath it in the International Phonetic Alphabet, Wiktionary's own. The 729 nouns are printed with their article — de or het — because nothing in a Dutch noun says which it takes, and they show their plural and diminutive; the 427 verbs show their past and past participle (eten, at, gegeten), and behind the All forms fold their present and past by person, imperative and participles. Real example sentences come with 1422 of the 1500 words, three apiece for 1251 of them, with the word picked out in colour and a speaker beside the sentence and the headword. Sources. Level: the Common European Framework of Reference (Council of Europe), global scale. Meanings, gender, forms and pronunciation: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0). Frequency: a word list built from OpenSubtitles (hermitdave/FrequencyWords, CC BY-SA 4.0). Example sentences: Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.
